label: USE CASE 04
title: How Netflix and YouTube Recommend Videos

scenes.text: You finish one video, and the next one is somehow exactly what you wanted. [1] So how do YouTube and Netflix know your taste so well? [2] Let's break down recommendation systems.

It all starts with signals, basically everything you do. [1] What you watch, and for how long. [2] What you like, share or skip. [3] What people similar to you enjoyed. [4] All of this is turned into numbers, [5] and the system predicts what you're most likely to watch next.

Here's the key idea, from episode six. [1] Both you and every video get an embedding, a spot on a map of taste. Comedy here, cricket there, cooking over there. [2] Your profile lands on the map, based on what you watch. [3] And the closest videos become your recommendations.

data.heading: A map of taste
data.note: Watch cooking videos, get more cooking videos

scenes.text: Big platforms do this in two stages. [1] First, they pick candidates. From millions of videos, they quickly pick a few hundred that might suit you. [2] Then comes ranking, where a bigger model scores each one carefully, and puts them in order. [3] And finally, they mix in a little variety, so you also see something fresh.

Here are four terms you'll hear. [1] Collaborative filtering, which means people like you liked this. [2] Content based, which means this is similar to what you watched. [3] Watch time, one of the strongest signals of all. [4] And the cold start problem, when a new user or a new video has no history yet.
And this is everywhere. [1] YouTube and Netflix choose your next video. [2] Amazon and Flipkart suggest products. [3] And Spotify builds your daily mixes.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think apps listen to their conversations to recommend things. [2] Usually, they don't need to. What you watch, search and click, plus what similar people do, is enough to predict you surprisingly well.

data.myth: Apps listen to my conversations to recommend things.
data.fact: They usually don't need to. Your clicks, searches and similar people predict you surprisingly well.
